entries.seminar_title: Temps and Extreme Temps: The Effect of Extreme Temperature on Temporary Labor
entries.speaker: Cameron Scalera
entries.abstract: We provide the first study of how extreme temperature shocks affect establishment use of temporary labor. We focus on U.S. manufacturing, a sector in which temporary labor has been rising and for which temperature shocks could affect both labor supply and demand. We build a conceptual model that illustrates mechanisms and shows how the net effect of extreme temperature on temporary labor is theoretically ambiguous. We then estimate net effects empirically using reduced-form methods and exploiting exogenous extremes in daily temperature. Initial results show that extreme temperatures increase the number and percent of workers in the temporary services industry and more so in areas with high shares of manufacturing employment. These results have important implications for how firms adapt to economic shocks, such as from climate change, and how these shocks are distributed across different types of workers.

entries.seminar_title: Heterogeneous Agency? Perceived Returns to Effort and Earnings Inequality
entries.speaker: Kathryn McDonald
Jean Tirole
entries.abstract: Perceived commonality—rooted in shared interests, parochial altruism, durable relationships, or common priors—is a critical lubricant of collective action in both organizations and societies. Cohesion emerges when organizations cultivate narratives of shared purpose, regulate acceptable discourse, and foster interpersonal bonding. This paper develops a framework in which two team members’ engagement rises with their perceived congruence, and payoffs are represented by a convex-concave function of that congruence The agents learn about each other through i.i.d. experiments. The analysis first characterizes the optimal level of information acquisition through public experiments from each player’s perspective. It then studies the strategic communication game that unfolds when information sharing is unmediated. The equilibrium outcome depends critically on the nature of the information: when information is hard, the equilibrium favors the less information averse agent; when it is soft, it favors—at best—the other agent.

entries.seminar_title: The Welfare Effects of Traffic Calming: Evidence from London’s 20 mph Limits
entries.speaker: Stephan Thies
entries.abstract: Traffic calming, such as 20 mph speed limits, road closures, and low traffic neighborhoods, has become a popular tool in many cities to reduce road accidents and to curb the local externalities of motor vehicle traffic. Yet traffic calming is often contested as it can increase travel times for drivers. Unlike Pigouvian pricing, which has received substantial attention in the economics literature but is rarely implemented to regulate traffic, traffic calming has a priori ambiguous welfare consequences. This paper studies these trade-offs empirically in the context of Greater London. Combining GPS data with roadside monitors, I assemble a novel dataset tracking annual vehicle volumes and speeds on every road in London between 2010 and 2025. I document that during this period average speeds fell by about 10% despite declining traffic volumes. Exploiting the staggered rollout of 20 mph limits, I estimate how much the lower limits contribute to the decline, their effect on road collisions, and how they redistribute traffic across the network. I combine these estimates with hedonic estimates of residents’ willingness to pay for quieter, slower streets to quantify the net welfare effect of the policy and its distribution across neighborhoods.
